The Niemeier gap: Coxeter numbers modulo 16

The 23 root systems of rank 24 with one Coxeter number h, in the column h mod 16. No tile ever lands in columns 1, 11, 15. A picture shows a structure; it is not evidence that the structure means anything beyond its definition.

The control. Is it surprising that the Moonshine primes fill the gap? Every 14-subset of the 19 odd primes up to 71 (the 14 odd Moonshine primes are one of them), counted exactly:
The proof, as data.
About this visual

What you are looking at. The 23 root systems of the Niemeier lattices: the ways to make an A/D/E root system of rank 24 whose pieces all share one Coxeter number h. Each tile is one root system, standing in the column of its h mod 16 (the sixteen sedenion places). Under the columns, the 15 Moonshine primes (those dividing the order of the Monster) stand in the column of p mod 16.

How to read it. Shaded columns are residues no tile reaches: the Niemeier gap. Switch the rank to see the same construction at another rank: the gap is a fact about 24 and 16, not about root systems in general. Switch Moonshine primes on to see them fall in the gap columns; the control card says how often a prime set of that size does that anyway.

What it shows. Theorem (proved in the engine): the gap is exactly {1, 11, 15}. An odd h forces every piece to be A(h−1), and then h−1 divides 24; so the odd h are 3, 5, 7, 9, 13, 25. The tiles are generated here, in the browser, from the defining condition and equal the Python engine's 23.

What it does not show. That the gap is a Fermat 'forbidden zone': no definition of such a zone as a set of solutions of x^p + y^q = z^r is in code, so that reading stays THEORETICAL. And the Moonshine fill is not evidence: 68% of 14-prime subsets of the odd primes up to 71 also cover all three gap residues.

Numbers to check. 23 root systems at rank 24; h in {2,…,10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 22, 25, 30, 46}; gap {1, 11, 15}. Control: 7,904 of 11,628 subsets cover the gap (68.0%), 5,283 cover all eight odd residues (45.4%).

Literature.

  • C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), §VII; P. L. Wantzel, "Recherches sur les moyens de reconnaître si un Problème de Géométrie peut se résoudre avec la règle et le compas", J. Math. Pures Appl. 2 (1837) 366–372. Constructibility of the regular n-gon.
  • H.-V. Niemeier, "Definite quadratische Formen der Dimension 24 und Diskriminante 1", J. Number Theory 5 (1973) 142–178.
  • J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups (Springer, 1999), ch. 16 and 18: the 24 Niemeier lattices and their Coxeter numbers; ch. 1: the volume of the n-ball.
  • A. P. Ogg, "Automorphismes de courbes modulaires", Séminaire Delange–Pisot–Poitou 16 (1974/75), exposé 7. The 15 primes dividing the order of the Monster.
  • A. N. Schellekens, "Meromorphic c = 24 conformal field theories", Commun. Math. Phys. 153 (1993) 159–185. The 71 holomorphic c = 24 theories.
  • P. J. Davis, "Leonhard Euler's Integral: A Historical Profile of the Gamma Function", Amer. Math. Monthly 66 (1959) 849–869.
  • G. Veneziano, "Construction of a crossing-symmetric, Regge-behaved amplitude for linearly rising trajectories", Nuovo Cimento A 57 (1968) 190–197. The amplitude was Euler's beta function, Γ(a)Γ(b)/Γ(a+b).
  • H. Darmon and A. Granville, "On the equations z^m = F(x, y) and Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r", Bull. London Math. Soc. 27 (1995) 513–543; F. Beukers, "The Diophantine equation Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r", Duke Math. J. 91 (1998) 61–88. Where generalized Fermat meets the ADE (spherical) signatures.
  • The Python Software Foundation, Python 3 documentation: math.lgamma, math.gamma.
  • OpenSCAD User Manual (camera, projection, multmatrix).
  • MDN Web Docs, Canvas API.
